clue.text: Omar's favourite purveyor?

parts.note: Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat wonders what wine-sellers buy one half so precious as the stuff they sell

explanation.surface: A question about which shopkeeper the Persian poet Omar liked best.
explanation.walkthrough: In FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the poet says he often wonders what the vintners buy one half so precious as the stuff they sell; wine is his constant theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A vintner is a wine merchant, the supplier the wine-loving poet would favour.

clue.text: Suitable head-pieces, if small, for 1 ac.

definitions.text: Suitable head-pieces, if small, for 1 ac.

parts.words: Suitable head-pieces, if small, for 1 ac.
parts.note: small decorative designs at the head of a book's chapter, originally of vine leaves, which would suit the wine merchant of 1 across

explanation.surface: Small decorations that would suit a wine merchant's book.
explanation.walkthrough: A vignette, from French vigne (vine), was first a vine-leaf ornament heading a page, so it suits the vintner of 1 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A vignette is a small ornamental design at a chapter head, named from its original vine tendrils.

clue.text: Distinguished or inefficient?

explanation.surface: Someone either eminent or incompetent.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as NOT ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguished people are eminent and worthy of note; read as two words it means incapable.

clue.text: A short drink for chela's relative

parts.note: a chela is a crab's claw, which is a nipper
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: A small drink for the relation of a disciple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chela' also means a Buddhist disciple, as in Kipling's Kim, which is the sense the surface plays on; here it is the claw.
explanation.definitionFit: A nipperkin is an old measure holding a small quantity of liquor, half a pint or less.

clue.text: Barbary for Richard

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Richard II the king's horse is called Barbary, and its colour is named with it

explanation.surface: A note about Richard and the Barbary coast.
explanation.walkthrough: In Richard II, the groom speaks of 'roan Barbary', the horse Bolingbroke rode at his coronation, once the king's own.
explanation.definitionFit: Roan describes a horse whose coat is mixed with white hairs, the colour of Richard's mount.

clue.text: Chap's got a short way to make this roof

parts.note: a chap is a man, and the possessive gives the S
RD is the short form of road, a way

explanation.surface: A man builds a roof using a short road.
explanation.definitionFit: A mansard is a type of roof with two slopes on each side, the lower one steep.

clue.text: Doubts when a girl's yielding at heart

indicators.note: the yielding word sits at the centre of the girl word

parts.note: a miss is a girl, the possessive supplying the final S
giving means yielding, as a support gives under weight

explanation.surface: A girl's inner yielding raises doubts.
explanation.definitionFit: Misgivings are feelings of doubt or apprehension.

clue.text: "And dark and true and tender is the ——" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "And dark and true and tender is the ——" (Tennyson)

parts.words: "And dark and true and tender is the ——" (Tennyson)
parts.note: a line from the song O Swallow, Swallow in Tennyson's The Princess, contrasting a direction with the fickle south

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's The Princess contains 'O tell her, Swallow, that thy brood is flown... And dark and true and tender is the North'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem sets the faithful northern lands against the bright, fickle south.

clue.text: In a delineation you may find a sweet girl

indicators.note: the girl's name sits inside the letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A drawing in which a lovely girl appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet Adeline' is a popular old barbershop song.
explanation.definitionFit: Adeline is a girl's name, made familiar by the song 'Sweet Adeline'.

clue.text: Orders, man to leave fruit

indicators.note: the man word departs from the orders word

parts.note: mandates are official orders

explanation.surface: Orders for a man to leave some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking MAN from MANDATES leaves DATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Dates are the sweet fruit of the date palm.

clue.text: Rise and dress

explanation.surface: Getting out of bed and putting clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise from bed is to get up; an outfit or costume is a getup.

clue.text: An eye in a faraway manner taking it all in

indicators.note: the eye piece goes inside the word for a faraway manner

parts.note: an absent manner is distracted, faraway
an orb is a poetic word for an eye

explanation.surface: A dreamy-looking person whose eyes nonetheless miss nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text reads 'oye'; the printed page has 'eye'. 'taking it all in' sounds like attentive watching but means soaking up liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absorbent soaks up liquid entirely, drawing it all into itself.

clue.text: "And spades, the —— of untimely graves" (Cowper)

parts.note: a line from Cowper's poem The Task describing the card suit of spades as a symbol of early death

explanation.surface: A line of Cowper's verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from William Cowper's The Task, where the card-playing passage calls spades the token of untimely graves.
explanation.definitionFit: A spade suggests digging graves, so the suit stands as a symbol or token of them.

clue.text: In these it's warm for the elderly

definitions.text: In these it's warm for the elderly

parts.words: In these it's warm for the elderly
parts.note: temperatures in the high Fahrenheit range feel warm, and old people may be aged in that decade of life

explanation.surface: A remark that old people find a certain range of weather pleasantly warm.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of a decade number: a temperature of 80 to 89 degrees Fahrenheit is warm weather, and the elderly may be in that decade of age.
explanation.definitionFit: The decade from eighty to eighty-nine covers both warm Fahrenheit readings and the age of many old people.

clue.text: Where, tardily, to conceal the illicit cigarette ?

definitions.text: Where, tardily, to conceal the illicit cigarette ?

parts.words: Where, tardily, to conceal the illicit cigarette ?
parts.note: a forbidden smoke is hidden at your back in your palm, and the phrase for that hiding place also means late

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's question about where to hide a forbidden cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is the hiding place, behind one's hand; as one word it means late, which 'tardily' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Being late or in arrears is being behind schedule, like a slow payer.

clue.text: Pinch hardwood out of the West

indicators.note: the wood comes out around the abbreviation, enclosing it

parts.note: teak is a tropical hardwood
W is the abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: Stealing hardwood from the western states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinch' looks like steal, to go with 'hardwood out of the West', but means a small sharp twist.
explanation.definitionFit: To pinch someone's nose or ear is to give it a twisting nip, a small sharp tug.

clue.text: I blaze the trail for her

indicators.note: the words are dragged about, trailed into another order

explanation.surface: Someone pioneering a path on a woman's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blaze the trail' reads as a single idiom, but 'trail' is the anagram signal working on I BLAZE THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth is a woman's name, so 'her' stands for any female person.

clue.text: Woolly-minded sailors

parts.note: suggests vague, muddled seamen, but means crew whose minds were set on wool, the Golden Fleece

explanation.surface: A crew of confused sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woolly-minded' suggests muddled thinking; Jason's crew sailed the Argo in quest of the Golden Fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason's crew aboard the Argo sailed to fetch the Golden Fleece, a ram's wool.

clue.text: Crowned as Bacchus

parts.note: the god of wine is shown wearing a wreath of ivy, Latin hedera

explanation.surface: Someone crowned like the god of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacchus is pictured wreathed with ivy, Latin hedera.
explanation.definitionFit: Hederated means wreathed or crowned with ivy, the plant sacred to the wine god.

clue.text: "And I would turn and answer Among the —— thyme" (Housman)

definitions.text: "And I would turn and answer Among the —— thyme" (Housman)

parts.words: "And I would turn and answer Among the —— thyme" (Housman)
parts.note: a line from Housman's A Shropshire Lad, in the poem about lying on a hillside answering the cuckoo, with one adjective missing before thyme

explanation.surface: A line of Housman's poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue lost its gap mark; the page shows the blank before 'thyme'. Housman's line reads 'Among the springing thyme'.
explanation.definitionFit: Springing means sprouting or growing fresh, describing the young thyme in the poem's spring hillside.

clue.text: Time ran wild in gear

indicators.note: the words run wild, scattering into a new order

explanation.surface: Time racing out of control while in a particular gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gear' suggests a car's gearbox, but means clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is clothing; gear is an informal word for clothes.

clue.text: As a matador might, thus embarrassed by a bull

definitions.text: As a matador might, thus embarrassed by a bull

parts.words: As a matador might, thus embarrassed by a bull
parts.note: a bullfighter may end up pierced by the horns; embarrassed is used in its old sense of hampered or hurt

explanation.surface: A matador suffering an awkward moment in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embarrassed' points to social discomfort; the matador's real trouble is a horn wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull that pierces someone with its horns has wounded them in exactly that way.

clue.text: Steely answer ?

parts.note: a reply made with a steel blade, as a fencer's return thrust

explanation.surface: A cold, hard reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steely' suggests a cold tone, but means made with a steel sword: a fencer's return thrust after parrying.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is both a quick retort and a fencer's counter-thrust after a parry.

clue.text: Woman patient

parts.note: suggests a female hospital case, but names the proverbially long-suffering wife of medieval tale

explanation.surface: A woman waiting in a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patient' looks like a noun, a person under treatment; it is the adjective, as in 'patient Griselda', the wife in Boccaccio and Chaucer who endured every trial.
explanation.definitionFit: The wife in Chaucer's Clerk's Tale is the byword for a long-suffering, uncomplaining woman.

clue.text: Inflationary words and then more come in spasms

parts.note: gas is empty talk, words that puff things up
PS, postscript, adds more after a letter

explanation.surface: Puffed-up talk followed by more, coming in fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasps are sudden convulsive catches of breath.

clue.text: A small place in the jewellery department

indicators.note: the place name sits inside the letters of the longer word

explanation.surface: A small spot in a jewellery department.
explanation.walkthrough: EWELL is a small town in Surrey, south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewell is a small town in Surrey, near Epsom.

clue.text: Single-minded sportsman ?

parts.note: a hunter who picks off one target at a time, as in shooting the small wading bird

explanation.surface: An athlete wholly focused on winning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single-minded' suggests dedication; here it means one shot at one target, as a marksman shoots snipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A marksman who shoots from cover picks off single targets; originally one who shot snipe.

clue.text: Dress for a small copper

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
d stood for a penny, a copper coin in old British money

explanation.surface: Clothes for a little policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' suggests a policeman; it is the penny, D in pre-1971 British money. WEED here is an old word for a garment, as in widow's weeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A weed is an archaic word for a garment, surviving in widow's weeds.

clue.text: Nightfall in the coach making for town

indicators.note: the nightfall word goes inside the coach word

parts.note: a stagecoach is shortened to stage
even, as in evening or e'en, is the poetic word for nightfall

explanation.surface: Travelling by coach towards a town as night falls.
explanation.walkthrough: STEVENAGE is a town in Hertfordshire, north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenage is an English new town in Hertfordshire.

clue.text: Conversely this spill can right itself

definitions.text: Conversely this spill can right itself

parts.words: Conversely this spill can right itself
parts.note: a word for an overturning becomes, with its two halves swapped round, a phrase meaning to put back upright

explanation.surface: Something knocked over that manages to stand up again.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the halves of the word for a spill and you get SET UP, which means to put right.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset something is to knock it over, spilling its contents.

clue.text: Installed on the bench?

explanation.surface: A judge newly appointed to the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the bench' suggests a judge; a settle is a high-backed wooden bench, so to be on one is to be settled.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone installed in a new home is settled; a settle is a wooden bench to sit on.

clue.text: Does Pluto incline to swell?

parts.note: Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld
to tend is to incline towards something

explanation.surface: Asking whether the god Pluto tends to get puffed up.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text reads 'cine'; the printed page has 'incline'.
explanation.definitionFit: To distend is to stretch out or bloat from pressure within.
